key_points: Monitoring Systems Abstract Physiological anomaly detection is an important application in the early diagnosis of health risks and unusual bodily conditions.

Conventional machine learning methods tend to use centralized processing and static models, which might not be adaptable to individual- specific physiological variations and could pose privacy and latency issues.

This paper proposes an adaptive on-device DQN framework for physiological anomaly detection, with a focus on a new reward adjustment mechanism that can adaptively adjust to varying physiological patterns.

Instead of making a new algorithmic contribution, the novelty of the proposed method is in combining on-device learning constraints with an adaptive reward mechanism that can enhance anomaly detection sensitivity and personalization.
The proposed method is tested with physiological signal data under simulated device conditions and shows its feasibility and efficacy.
The experimental results show that adaptive reward adjustment can improve detection performance over static reward mechanisms.

key_points: Introduction The availability of physiological data through wearable and personal monitoring systems has made it possible to continuously monitor health and detect anomalies early. Heart rate and other physiological signals are useful for gaining insights into the physiological state of an individual. However, it is difficult to detect anomalies in these signals because of the high variability among individuals, noise, and non-stationarity. Most of the existing methods use supervised or unsupervised learning models that are trained in centralized settings. Although these methods are efficient, they are not adaptable to individual-level changes and pose privacy issues when personal health data is sent to cloud servers. Furthermore, traditional models are not capable of handling dynamic physiological changes due to stress, activity, or health changes. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a promising technique that allows systems to learn from interactions and feedback received from the environment. RL is particularly suitable for dealing with temporal dependencies as well as adapting decision-making policies over time. In recent years, on-device learning has emerged as a promising solution for dealing with challenges associated with latency, data privacy, and adaptation. This paper describes an adaptive on-device reinforcement learning framework for physiological anomaly detection using Deep Q-Learning (DQN). The main contribution of this paper does not lie in the development of a new algorithm but in the effective combination of on-device reinforcement learning with a reward function dynamically adjusted according to the characteristics of physiological signals. The proposed adaptive approach allows the system to adapt to changing signal patterns while being subject to practical device-level computational limitations.

key_points: Related Work Reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied in several healthcare-oriented studies to enable adaptive and personalized decision-making. Yom-Tov et al. employed Q-learning to encourage physical activity among diabetes patients through personalized goal settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive feedback in influencing user behavior. Other research has utilized Q-learning in Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) to improve energy efficiency by optimizing sensor data transmission, focusing primarily on system- level performance rather than health data interpretation. Reinforcement learning has also been explored for time-series anomaly detection, where RL-based and active learning methods adaptively identify anomalous patterns in sequential data. Additionally, recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning based dynamic health monitoring frameworks that adjust monitoring strategies based on user activity; however, such approaches often rely on complex models and non-physiological inputs, such as video data, which limit their applicability in resource-constrained environments. Overall, existing works either emphasize behavioral intervention, communication efficiency, or computationally intensive architectures, leaving a gap in lightweight, on-device reinforcement learning approaches specifically designed for physiological anomaly detection.
